o: We have a `Variables` table mapping variable names to integer values, and an `Expressions` table where each row is a comparison `left_operand operator right_operand` with operator in `<`, `>`, `=`. We must evaluate each expression by looking up both operands' values and outputting the string `true` or `false`. In the example, `x > y` becomes `66 > 77` → `false`, while `y > x` → `true` and `x = x` → `true`. Since every operand is guaranteed to exist in `Variables`, a simple join suffices; no null handling or missing-value logic is needed. The main subtleties are joining the same table twice (once per operand) and formatting booleans as lowercase strings.
k: Join `Expressions` to `Variables` twice under different aliases: once for the left operand, once for the right.
CASE WHEN (or IF) on the joined values produces the boolean result; format it as the literal strings 'true'/'false'.
Because operands are guaranteed present, an INNER JOIN is safe and simpler than LEFT JOIN.

a.n: Approach 1: Double self-join with CASE expression
a.i: Treat each operand as a lookup into `Variables`. By aliasing `Variables` as `v1` (matched on `left_operand`) and `v2` (matched on `right_operand`), each expression row gains access to both numeric values. A CASE WHEN chain then compares them according to the operator column and emits 'true' or 'false'. This is the natural, optimal solution for a database problem — one pass over the join.
s: JOIN Variables v1 ON v1.name = e.left_operand to fetch the left value.
JOIN Variables v2 ON v2.name = e.right_operand to fetch the right value.
Use CASE WHEN e.operator = '<' AND v1.value < v2.value THEN 'true' ... ELSE 'false' END to compute the result.
Select the three original columns plus the computed value.

c.python:
# This problem is SQL-only on LeetCode; no Python class Solution exists.
# MySQL solution:
"""
SELECT e.left_operand, e.operator, e.right_operand,
       CASE
         WHEN e.operator = '<' AND v1.value < v2.value THEN 'true'
         WHEN e.operator = '>' AND v1.value > v2.value THEN 'true'
         WHEN e.operator = '=' AND v1.value = v2.value THEN 'true'
         ELSE 'false'
       END AS value
FROM Expressions e
JOIN Variables v1 ON v1.name = e.left_operand
JOIN Variables v2 ON v2.name = e.right_operand;
"""

a.t: O(E + V) expected — hash-index joins on primary keys touch each expression row once.
a.sp: O(E) for the output rows; join buffers are O(1) extra beyond input.

a.i: Instead of a verbose CASE chain, evaluate the whole condition as one boolean and convert it to text. In MySQL, `IF(condition, 'true', 'false')` collapses all three operators into a single line. Some engines also allow casting a boolean to a string directly. Same join structure, just terser projection logic.
s: Perform the same two joins against Variables as in Approach 1.
Build one combined predicate: (operator='<' AND v1.value<v2.value) OR (operator='>' AND ...) OR (operator='=' AND ...).
Wrap it in IF(..., 'true', 'false') to produce the value column.

c.python:
# MySQL solution:
"""
SELECT e.left_operand, e.operator, e.right_operand,
       IF((e.operator = '<' AND v1.value < v2.value) OR
          (e.operator = '>' AND v1.value > v2.value) OR
          (e.operator = '=' AND v1.value = v2.value), 'true', 'false') AS value
FROM Expressions e
JOIN Variables v1 ON v1.name = e.left_operand
JOIN Variables v2 ON v2.name = e.right_operand;
"""

a.t: O(E + V) — identical join cost to Approach 1; only the projection differs.

w: In an interview, go straight to the double-join solution — it is already optimal for this data model. Pitfalls: forgetting that the same table must be joined twice with distinct aliases (joining once loses one side's value); returning boolean literals like TRUE instead of the required lowercase strings 'true'/'false'; and using LEFT JOIN unnecessarily when operands are guaranteed present. Edge cases are minimal here since operands always resolve, but note that equal values make both `<` and `>` false while `=` is true. Likely follow-ups: extend operators to `<=`, `>=`, `!=` (just add CASE branches), handle chained expressions (recursive CTEs), or deal with missing variables (switch to LEFT JOIN with NULL handling).
